title: Behavioral Design Patterns
description: Observer, Strategy, Command, State, Chain of Responsibility, Template Method, Mediator, Iterator, Memento, and Visitor.

topics.title: Observer Pattern & Event Dispatchers
topics.description: Defining a one-to-many dependency so that when one object changes state, all dependents are notified automatically.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: The Observer Pattern (Publish-Subscribe) maintains a list of dependents and notifies them automatically of state changes by calling their update() method.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Decouples event producers from consumers; producers don't need to know concrete subscriber types.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Subject has attach(observer), detach(observer), and notifyObservers().

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: When subject state changes, it iterates through its registered observer list calling obs->update().

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

callout.title: Observer Publish Flow
callout.text: StockTicker::setPrice(150.0) -> notifyObservers() -> updates PhoneApp, WebDashboard, TradingBot

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: StockTicker notifies all registered IObserver instances automatically upon price mutation.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: GUI event listeners (button clicks), Message brokers (Kafka, RabbitMQ), Reactive Extensions (RxCpp).

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use whenever changes in one object require updating an open-ended set of other objects.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not use when observer notification chains can create circular update loops.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Loose coupling between subject and observers; broadcast communication.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Subscribers can leak memory if not properly detached before destruction (Lapsed Listener problem).

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Push Model (Subject pushes data), Pull Model (Subject sends reference, observer pulls).

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Forgetting to unsubscribe observers before destruction causing dangling callbacks.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: How do you prevent the Lapsed Listener memory leak in C++ Observer implementations?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: Store observers as std::weak_ptr<IObserver> in the subject's collection. If an observer is deleted, lock() returns null and the subject cleans it up automatically.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Implement WeatherStation notifying PhoneDisplay and StatsDisplay on temperature change.

practice.title: Weather Station Observer
practice.problemStatement: Implement WeatherStation notifying PhoneDisplay and StatsDisplay on temperature change.

referenceCode.code: class WeatherStation { vector<shared_ptr<IObserver>> obs; public: void setTemp(double t) { for(auto& o: obs) o->update(t); } };

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Mastering Observer Pattern & Event Dispatchers is essential for advanced Low-Level Design interviews.

topics.title: Strategy Pattern & Interchangeable Algorithms
topics.description: Defining a family of algorithms, encapsulating each one, and making them interchangeable at runtime.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: The Strategy Pattern lets the algorithm vary independently from clients that use it by encapsulating algorithms into distinct classes.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Eliminates giant if-else/switch blocks for payment calculations, routing algorithms, and compression formats.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Context class contains a pointer to IStrategy and delegates computation to it.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: navigator.setRouteStrategy(new FastestRoute()) switches algorithm dynamically at runtime.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

callout.title: Strategy Interchangeability
callout.text: PaymentProcessor -> executes strategy->pay() -> works with CreditCard, PayPal, UPI, Crypto

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: DataContext swaps between QuickSortStrategy and MergeSortStrategy seamlessly.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Sorting algorithms, compression formats (GZIP vs ZSTD), routing path algorithms in GPS navigation.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use when you have multiple variants of an algorithm that should be selectable at runtime.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not use if an algorithm never changes and only one implementation will ever exist.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Adheres to Open/Closed Principle; eliminates conditional switch logic.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Clients must be aware of differences between strategies to select the right one.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Object-Oriented Strategy, Modern C++ Functional Strategy (using std::function).

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Passing large context state unnecessarily to simple stateless strategies.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: How can the Strategy Pattern be implemented using modern C++ lambdas?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: By replacing the strategy interface hierarchy with std::function<double(double)>, allowing callers to pass inline lambdas directly without class boilerplate.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Implement FileArchiver using ZipCompression and RarCompression strategies.

practice.title: Compression Strategy
practice.problemStatement: Implement FileArchiver using ZipCompression and RarCompression strategies.

referenceCode.code: class ICompress { public: virtual ~ICompress() = default; virtual void compress() = 0; };

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Mastering Strategy Pattern & Interchangeable Algorithms is essential for advanced Low-Level Design interviews.

topics.title: Command Pattern & Undo/Redo Architecture
topics.description: Encapsulating a request as an object, enabling parameterization with queues, logs, and undoable operations.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: The Command Pattern turns a request into a stand-alone object containing all information about the request (receiver, method, arguments), enabling undo/redo, queuing, and transaction logging.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Directly executing mutations makes undo/redo and background job queuing impossible.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: ICommand defines execute() and undo().

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: An Invoker maintains a history stack of executed commands. Calling Undo pops the top command and executes cmd->undo().

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

callout.title: Command Stack
callout.text: CommandHistory: [TypeCommand('A'), TypeCommand('B'), DeleteCommand()] -> Undo() -> calls DeleteCommand::undo()

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: CommandManager tracks InsertTextCommand history stack supporting execute and undo.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Text editor undo/redo, GUI button action bindings, transactional rollback systems, thread pool task queues.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use for undo/redo, task scheduling, asynchronous job queues, and macro recording.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not use for simple direct method invocations with no queuing or undo needs.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Decouples invoker from receiver; enables reversible operations.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Increases number of command classes.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Undoable Command, Macro Command (Composite Command), Asynchronous Task Command.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Failing to capture complete state required to accurately undo the operation.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: How is Command pattern used to implement Transactional Rollbacks?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: Each database mutation is wrapped in a Command object with execute() committing SQL and undo() issuing compensating rollback queries in reverse execution order.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Implement LightOnCommand and LightOffCommand for a remote control invoker.

practice.title: Smart Home Remote Command
practice.problemStatement: Implement LightOnCommand and LightOffCommand for a remote control invoker.

referenceCode.code: class ICommand { public: virtual ~ICommand() = default; virtual void execute() = 0; };

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Mastering Command Pattern & Undo/Redo Architecture is essential for advanced Low-Level Design interviews.

topics.title: State Pattern & Finite State Machines
topics.description: Allowing an object to alter its behavior when its internal state changes, appearing to change its class.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: The State Pattern encapsulates state-specific behavior inside separate state classes, eliminating massive switch-case state machines.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: When an object's behavior depends heavily on its state, adding new states requires editing giant conditional blocks across every method.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Context contains a pointer to IState and delegates state-dependent actions to state->handle().

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: State methods transition the Context to a new IState instance upon valid triggers.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

callout.title: State Pattern Structure
callout.text: TCPConnection -> state->open() -> If ClosedState: transitions to SynSentState. If EstablishedState: throws error.

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: DocumentContext delegates publish() to DraftState -> ModerationState -> PublishedState.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: TCP connection lifecycles, Order processing state machines, Vending machines, Game character states (Idle, Run, Jump, Attack).

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use when an object has complex state-dependent behaviors with many state transitions.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not use if the object only has 2 simple states with minimal logic.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Eliminates monolithic switch-cases; encapsulates state transitions cleanly.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Increases class count.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: State with Context back-reference, Stateless Shared States.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Allowing transitions from terminal states.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: What is the difference between State and Strategy patterns?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: Structure is identical, but Intent differs: Strategy provides interchangeable algorithms chosen by the client. State manages dynamic lifecycle transitions controlled by internal events.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Implement NoCoinState, HasCoinState, and SoldState.

referenceCode.code: class IState { public: virtual ~IState() = default; virtual void insertCoin() = 0; };

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Mastering State Pattern & Finite State Machines is essential for advanced Low-Level Design interviews.

topics.title: Chain of Responsibility Pattern
topics.description: Passing requests along a chain of potential handlers until one of them handles it.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: Chain of Responsibility decouples the sender of a request from its receivers by giving multiple objects a chance to handle the request sequentially.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Hardcoding request dispatchers creates tight coupling between callers and all possible handler classes.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Each handler holds a pointer to nextHandler in the chain.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: handle(request) checks if it can process the request; if yes, it executes; if no, it forwards to nextHandler->handle(request).

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: ConsoleLoggerHandler and ErrorFileLoggerHandler chain log processing sequentially.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: HTTP Request Middleware filters, Technical Support escalation tiers (L1 -> L2 -> L3), GUI event bubbling.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use when multiple objects can handle a request and the exact handler isn't known up-front.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not use when every request must be handled by a single deterministic method.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Loose coupling between sender and receivers; dynamic chain configuration.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: A request can fall off the end of the chain unhandled.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Terminating Chain (first handler stops), Pass-Through Chain (all handlers process).

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Creating circular chain references causing infinite loops.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: How is Chain of Responsibility used in web server middleware?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: Each middleware layer (Authentication -> Rate Limiting -> CORS -> Logging -> Handler) executes preprocessing, calls next.handle(), and executes postprocessing.

sections.content: Build L1Support, L2Support, and L3Support ticket handlers.

practice.problemStatement: Build L1Support, L2Support, and L3Support ticket handlers.

sections.content: Mastering Chain of Responsibility Pattern is essential for advanced Low-Level Design interviews.

topics.title: Template Method Pattern
topics.description: Defining the skeleton of an algorithm in a base class, letting subclasses override specific steps without changing structure.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: Template Method defines the invariant skeleton of an algorithm in a base method, deferring some steps to subclasses.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Duplicating algorithm structure across subclasses while only 1 or 2 steps differ leads to code duplication.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Base class defines a final or non-virtual template method calling private/protected virtual step hooks.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Subclasses override the hook methods; the base template method coordinates the execution sequence.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

callout.title: Hollywood Principle
callout.text: 'Don't call us, we'll call you.' The base class algorithm calls the derived class hooks, not the other way around!

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: DataMiner::mineData() coordinates the execution skeleton while PdfDataMiner overrides extraction steps.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Game loop update lifecycles, Data ETL pipelines, Build system build stages (compile -> test -> package).

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use when multiple classes share an identical multi-step workflow where only individual steps vary.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not use when the entire workflow structure varies between subclasses.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Eliminates code duplication; enforces standard workflow sequence.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Subclasses are tightly coupled to base class algorithm order.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Template Method with Hooks, Pure Virtual Template Steps.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Overriding the main template method in subclasses and breaking workflow invariants.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: Why is the template method in the base class usually non-virtual or final?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: To prevent subclasses from overriding and corrupting the overarching execution sequence of the algorithm.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Implement GameTurn template method calling startTurn(), takeAction(), and endTurn().

practice.title: Game Turn Template Method
practice.problemStatement: Implement GameTurn template method calling startTurn(), takeAction(), and endTurn().

referenceCode.code: class Turn { public: void play() { start(); act(); end(); } virtual void start() = 0; virtual void act() = 0; virtual void end() = 0; };

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Mastering Template Method Pattern is essential for advanced Low-Level Design interviews.

topics.title: Mediator Pattern & Loose Coupling
topics.description: Reducing chaotic dependencies between objects by forcing them to communicate through a central mediator object.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: The Mediator Pattern encapsulates how a set of objects interact, preventing chaotic many-to-many direct references (all-to-all coupling).

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: In an air traffic control network, 20 airplanes communicating directly with each other requires $O(N^2)$ communication links. A central control tower reduces links to $O(N)$.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Colleagues hold a reference to IMediator and send notifications through it.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: The Mediator receives events and orchestrates responses across other colleagues.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

callout.title: Many-to-Many vs Mediator
callout.text: Direct: 10 UI widgets talk directly to each other (100 coupling links!)\nMediator: 10 UI widgets talk ONLY to DialogMediator (10 links!)

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: ChatRoomMediator coordinates message delivery between Alice and Bob without direct coupling.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Air Traffic Control towers, Chat room servers, Complex UI Dialog forms.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use when a group of objects communicate in complex, tightly coupled many-to-many ways.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not use when objects only have simple one-to-one communication.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Decouples colleagues; centralizes interaction control.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: The Mediator can turn into a complex God Object.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Event Aggregator, UI Dialog Mediator.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Putting business calculation logic inside the mediator instead of keeping it in colleagues.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: What is the difference between Mediator and Observer?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: Observer is one-to-many unidirectional communication. Mediator is many-to-many bidirectional communication coordinating complex interactions across multiple colleagues.

sections.content: Build AirTrafficControl tower mediating landing runway access for Airplane colleagues.

practice.problemStatement: Build AirTrafficControl tower mediating landing runway access for Airplane colleagues.

referenceCode.code: class IATC { public: virtual void requestLanding(Airplane* a) = 0; };

sections.content: Mastering Mediator Pattern & Loose Coupling is essential for advanced Low-Level Design interviews.

topics.title: Iterator Pattern & Custom Iterators
topics.description: Accessing elements of an aggregate object sequentially without exposing its underlying representation.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: The Iterator Pattern provides a standard way to traverse elements of a collection sequentially without exposing its internal data structure (array, linked list, tree, hash map).

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Clients should not need to write different traversal algorithms depending on whether data is in a vector, binary tree, or linked list.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Iterator defines hasNext(), next(), or standard C++ operator++ and operator*.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: C++ Range-based for loops (for (auto& item : container)) work automatically by calling begin() and end() iterators.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

callout.title: C++ Standard Iterators
callout.text: Implementing operator*, operator++, and operator!= allows your custom container to work seamlessly with C++ range-based for loops and std::sort algorithms!

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: CustomList implements standard begin() and end() iterators enabling C++ range-based for loops.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: All C++ STL containers (std::vector, std::map, std::list), database cursor query iterators.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use when providing a clean, uniform traversal interface over complex internal collections.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not use if random index access (operator[]) is the only traversal pattern needed.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Decouples traversal algorithms from container data structures.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Writing bidirectional/random-access iterator boilerplate requires care.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Input, Output, Forward, Bidirectional, Random Access, and Contiguous Iterators.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Invalidating iterators by modifying the container during iteration without updating iterator pointers.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: What methods must a C++ class implement to support range-based for loops?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: It must provide begin() and end() methods returning an iterator type that implements operator*, prefix operator++, and operator!=.

sections.content: Implement a forward iterator for an in-order binary tree traversal.

practice.title: Binary Tree In-Order Iterator
practice.problemStatement: Implement a forward iterator for an in-order binary tree traversal.

sections.content: Mastering Iterator Pattern & Custom Iterators is essential for advanced Low-Level Design interviews.

topics.title: Memento Pattern (State Snapshots)
topics.description: Capturing and externalizing an object's internal state so it can be restored later without violating encapsulation.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: The Memento Pattern captures and stores the internal state of an object so that the object can be restored to this exact state later (Undo / Checkpointing).

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Exposing private fields to create backups violates encapsulation.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Originator creates Memento snapshot. Caretaker stores snapshots. Memento stores immutable state.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: originator.restoreFromMemento(caretaker.popSnapshot()).

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

callout.title: Memento Encapsulation
callout.text: The Memento object has private fields accessible ONLY by the Originator (via friend class), keeping internal state strictly hidden from the Caretaker!

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: CodeEditor creates and restores EditorMemento snapshots managed by HistoryCaretaker.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: IDE checkpoints, Game save files, Database transaction savepoints.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use for undo/redo and checkpoint rollback when state snapshotting is required.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not use if saving full object snapshots consumes excessive RAM (use command undo diffs instead).

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Preserves encapsulation while providing robust state restoration.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: High memory consumption if snapshots are frequent and large.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Full Memento Snapshot, Incremental Diff Memento.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Making Memento state public so other classes can tamper with internal state.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: How does Memento protect encapsulation in C++?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: By declaring the Originator as a friend class of the Memento and making all Memento constructors and fields private.

topics.title: Visitor Pattern & Double Dispatch
topics.description: Representing an operation to be performed on elements of an object structure without changing their classes.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: The Visitor Pattern lets you define a new operation on a collection of polymorphic objects without modifying their classes (Double Dispatch).

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Adding a new operation (e.g. ExportToXML, CalculateTaxes, RenderSVG) across 15 class types requires modifying all 15 classes.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Elements accept a visitor: element->accept(visitor), which double-dispatches: visitor->visit(this).

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: First dispatch: Virtual accept() on Element. Second dispatch: Overloaded visit() on Visitor.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

callout.title: Double Dispatch Flow
callout.text: Shape::accept(Visitor& v) { v.visit(*this); } -> Dynamic type of Shape + Overloaded type of Visitor resolved!

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: AreaCalculatorVisitor visits Circle and Rectangle polymorphically via double dispatch accept().

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Compiler Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) analyzers, Document format exporters (HTML, PDF, Markdown), Tax calculation engines.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use when an object structure rarely changes but you frequently need to add new operations over it.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not use if the object class hierarchy changes frequently (every new class breaks the visitor interface).

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Easy to add new operations; groups related operation logic together.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Extremely difficult to add new element classes to the hierarchy.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Classic Double-Dispatch Visitor, Acyclic Visitor, std::visit with std::variant (C++17).

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Forgetting to implement double dispatch and calling static overloads directly.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: What is Double Dispatch in C++ and how does Visitor achieve it?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: Double dispatch means the executed function depends on the runtime types of TWO objects. Visitor achieves it by first calling virtual element->accept(visitor) (first dispatch), which then calls visitor->visit(*this) (second dispatch).

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Implement a CodeGenVisitor traversing BinaryOpNode and NumberNode.

practice.title: AST Code Generator Visitor
practice.problemStatement: Implement a CodeGenVisitor traversing BinaryOpNode and NumberNode.

referenceCode.code: class IVisitor { public: virtual void visit(const BinaryOp&) = 0; virtual void visit(const Number&) = 0; };

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Mastering Visitor Pattern & Double Dispatch is essential for advanced Low-Level Design interviews.
